# Design WhatsApp

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `WhatsApp / Meta` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The hard part of WhatsApp isn't sending a message, it's that every single user might be connected right now on a flaky mobile network or not connected at all, so the entire architecture is really a distributed system for tracking '**who is reachable this instant**' and queuing for everyone who isn't.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a messaging system like WhatsApp: users exchange text messages
one-on-one, messages are delivered even if the recipient is offline when
they're sent, and the sender can see whether a message was sent, delivered
to the device, and read. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Is this one-on-one messaging only, or do we need group chats too?
*Why it matters:* Group chats turn a single delivery into a fan-out problem, similar in shape to timeline fan-out. Scoping to one-on-one first keeps the interview focused on connection management and delivery guarantees, which are the genuinely hard parts.

#### Q: Does the server need to be able to read message content, or is this end-to-end encrypted?
*Why it matters:* End-to-end encryption means the server can only ever store and forward opaque ciphertext blobs, it can never search, moderate, or generate previews of message content server-side. That constraint shapes the entire storage design, not just a security checkbox.

#### Q: What delivery guarantees do we need: sent, delivered to device, and read receipts, or just best-effort delivery?
*Why it matters:* Three distinct message states (sent, delivered, read) each require their own acknowledgment round trip and their own piece of state to track, which materially changes both the client protocol and the server's per-message bookkeeping.

#### Q: How long should messages be held for an offline recipient before we give up?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether the offline queue is a lightweight, bounded buffer or a durable long-term store, and it directly drives the storage capacity estimate.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can send a text message to another user.
- A message sent while the recipient is offline is queued and delivered once they reconnect.
- The sender can see message status: sent, delivered (reached the recipient's device), and read (opened by the recipient).
- A user can see their conversation history when they open a chat.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Message delivery must be near-real-time (sub-second) when both parties are online.**
- **The system must sustain hundreds of millions of concurrent open connections without falling over.**
- **No message should be silently lost: if the server accepted it, it must eventually be delivered or clearly reported as undeliverable.**
- **The system must tolerate a huge fraction of users being offline or on unreliable mobile networks at any given moment, without that degrading the experience for connected users.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 500 million daily active users, each with a persistent connection open while the app is in the foreground
- Average user sends 40 messages a day
- Peak concurrent connections are roughly 40% of DAU at once (evening peak across time zones)
- Each message (with metadata, before encryption overhead) is roughly 150 bytes

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Concurrent open connections at peak:** 500,000,000 * 0.4 = 200 million concurrent persistent connections to hold open at once
- **Connection gateway servers needed:** A single well-tuned server can hold roughly 500,000 to 1 million idle WebSocket connections; 200,000,000 / 500,000 = 400 gateway servers minimum, just to hold the sockets open
- **Messages sent per day and per second:** 500,000,000 * 40 = 20 billion messages/day ≈ 231,000 messages/sec average, several times that at peak
- **Daily storage for message history:** 20,000,000,000 * 150 bytes ≈ 3 TB/day of message data, ignoring media, which needs its own object storage path entirely

*Capacity Takeaway:* The number that actually drives this architecture isn't message throughput, it's the **200 million simultaneously open connections**: that single fact forces a horizontally sharded fleet of stateful gateway servers plus a routing layer that tracks which gateway holds which user's socket, which is a fundamentally different problem than a stateless request/response API.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Every client holds one persistent connection to a gateway server chosen by
a connection-aware load balancer. On connect, the gateway registers the
user's id against its own server id in a shared connection registry. When
user A sends a message to user B, A's gateway writes the message to
durable storage, then looks up B in the connection registry: if B is
connected somewhere, the message is pushed directly to B's gateway and
forwarded down B's socket in real time; if B is offline, the message id is
placed on B's offline queue instead. When B later reconnects, their
gateway drains the offline queue and pushes everything that piled up.
Delivered and read receipts flow back the same way, as small status
updates routed through the same registry back to A.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Connection gateways, routing registry, and offline queue

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    clienta["Client A"]:::client
    clientb["Client B (offline)"]:::client
    gwa["Gateway (A's socket)"]:::server
    gwb["Gateway (B's socket)"]:::server
    registry["Connection Registry"]:::cache
    msgdb[("Messages Store")]:::db
    offlineq>"Offline Queue"]:::queue
    clienta -->|"persistent WS"| gwa
    clientb -->|"persistent WS (down)"| gwb
    gwa -->|"store message"| msgdb
    gwa -->|"lookup recipient"| registry
    registry -->|"B offline"| gwa
    gwa -.->|"enqueue for B"| offlineq
    gwb -.->|"drain on reconnect"| offlineq
```

#### A message from send to read receipt

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. A sends message (over open socket to A's gateway)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Server stores message (status: sent, ack returned to A)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Registry lookup for B (online, or offline)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Push to B, or enqueue (delivered live, or queued for later)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. B's client acks delivered (status flows back to A)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. B opens the chat (status: read, flows back to A)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
```

#### Message status transitions

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  write["Server stores message"] -->|"ack to A"| sent["sent"]
  sent -->|"pushed to B's device"| delivered["delivered"]
  delivered -->|"B opens chat"| read["read"]
  sent -->|"B offline"| queued["queued"]
  queued -->|"B reconnects"| delivered
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `WS` | `wss://gateway/connect` | Upgrades to a persistent WebSocket connection, authenticates the user, and registers this connection in the presence/routing layer. |
| `POST` | `/api/messages` | Body: { recipient_id, ciphertext, client_message_id }. Sent over the open socket (or as a fallback HTTP call); the server acks with sent status and a server-assigned message_id. |
| `POST` | `/api/messages/{messageId}/ack` | Body: { status: 'delivered' | 'read' }. Sent by the recipient's client to report a status transition back to the server, which relays it to the original sender. |
| `GET` | `/api/conversations/{userId}/history` | Returns paginated message history for the conversation with userId, newest first, for populating the chat screen on open. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `messages`
- `message_id (unique, time-sortable)`
- `sender_id`
- `recipient_id`
- `ciphertext (opaque blob, server cannot read it)`
- `status (sent | delivered | read)`
- `created_at (timestamp)`
*Notes:* Sharded by conversation (a stable function of the two user IDs) so a whole conversation's history lives together for fast range reads.

### Entity: `offline_queue`
- `recipient_id (key)`
- `message_id`
- `enqueued_at`
*Notes:* A bounded, per-user queue of message IDs awaiting delivery. Drained and cleared the moment that user's client reconnects and acks receipt.

### Entity: `connection_registry`
- `user_id (key)`
- `gateway_server_id`
- `connected_at`
*Notes:* The routing table: which gateway server currently holds a given user's live socket. Kept in a fast in-memory store since it's read on every message send and rewritten on every connect/disconnect.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you route a message to a specific user when they could be connected to any one of thousands of gateway servers?
A stateless load balancer picking a random backend, as in a typical HTTP API, doesn't work here, because the recipient's live socket is pinned to one specific machine. The system needs a shared connection registry (commonly backed by something like Redis) mapping user_id to the gateway server holding their socket, so any gateway that needs to deliver to that user knows exactly which other gateway to forward to.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- **Shared connection registry** (lookup table in a fast store): any gateway can route to any user in one hop, but the registry itself must be highly available and consistent, since a stale entry means a message gets forwarded to a gateway that no longer holds that socket
- Consistent hashing of users to gateways (no lookup needed, user id determines gateway deterministically): removes the registry as a moving part, but rebalancing when gateways are added or removed forces many users to reconnect at once
- In practice, most large systems use the registry approach because connection churn (users reconnecting on flaky mobile networks constantly) makes a stable hash assignment hard to maintain cleanly

### How do sent, delivered, and read receipts actually work without adding a full extra round trip to every message?
Sent is acknowledged the moment the server durably stores the message, independent of the recipient. Delivered is acknowledged when the message reaches the recipient's device (their client sends a small ack back over its own socket the instant it receives the push). Read is acknowledged separately, only when the recipient actually opens that chat thread, which the client reports as its own event. Each status is a separate one-way ack message, not a blocking round trip on the original send.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Three independent async acks (current real-world approach): the sender's send is never blocked waiting on the recipient, each status update is just a small message flowing back through the same routing path
- A single synchronous 'confirm delivery before returning success' call: simpler mental model, but ties the sender's request latency to the recipient's network conditions, which is unacceptable when the recipient might be offline for hours
- Batching receipt acks (e.g. flush read receipts every few seconds instead of instantly): reduces small-message volume at high scale, at the cost of the sender's read receipt lagging by a few seconds, a trade-off most products accept for group chats but not for one-on-one

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The connection registry is read on every message send and written on every connect/disconnect, at hundreds of millions of entries; it needs to be sharded (by user_id) and run as a cluster, not a single instance, or it becomes the system's central bottleneck.
- A gateway server crashing instantly drops however many hundreds of thousands of connections it was holding; clients need exponential-backoff reconnect logic, and the registry must quickly detect and evict stale entries for that dead gateway so messages aren't routed into a black hole.
- The offline queue must be bounded per user (both in size and retention time), or a user who never reopens the app becomes an ever-growing storage liability; old queued messages past some retention window are dropped or the account is flagged.
- Because content is end-to-end encrypted, the server can't deduplicate, compress, or inspect messages meaningfully, so raw storage and bandwidth scale linearly with message volume with none of the usual content-aware optimizations available.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Designing this as if it were a stateless HTTP API== and forgetting that routing a message to a specific online user requires knowing exactly which server is holding their socket right now.
- ⚠️ ==Assuming delivered and read receipts can share a single status field==, when they're genuinely two separate events that happen at different times and need to be tracked and communicated independently.
- ⚠️ Not accounting for end-to-end encryption early, then proposing server-side features (search, spam filtering on content) that are simply impossible once the server can't read message bodies.
- ⚠️ Treating the offline queue as unbounded, which quietly becomes a storage time bomb for accounts that uninstall the app without ever reconnecting.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't a normal stateless load balancer route messages the way it routes typical API requests?**

> **Model Answer:** Because a typical stateless API request can be handled by any backend instance, but delivering a message to a specific online user requires reaching the exact gateway server that is holding that user's live socket right now. That requires a shared, fast-lookup registry mapping user to gateway, which a stateless load balancer has no concept of.

**Q: How would you handle a gateway server crashing with 500,000 open connections?**

> **Model Answer:** Clients detect the dropped socket and reconnect with exponential backoff (to avoid a reconnect stampede) to a newly assigned gateway via the load balancer. The connection registry needs a heartbeat or TTL mechanism so entries pointing at the dead gateway expire quickly, otherwise other gateways will keep trying to forward messages to a server that no longer exists.

# Design Slack

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Slack` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Slack looks like WhatsApp with channels bolted on, but the real design shift is that a channel isn't a conversation between two people, it's a **broadcast target** whose size varies from 2 to 50,000, and the right delivery strategy for a DM ==actively falls apart== at the top of that range.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a workspace-based team chat system like Slack: users belong to
organizations ("workspaces"), workspaces contain channels, users post

### How does search stay current without slowing down message sends?

- The async approach is the correct trade-off here because a brief indexing lag is invisible to users, while slow message sends are immediately and universally noticeable

- Very large channels remain the sharpest edge case; the threshold for switching from live-push to pull-on-open fan-out needs to be tuned against actual gateway push throughput, similar to the celebrity-account threshold in a feed system.

- ⚠️ ==Applying the same live-push fan-out strategy uniformly== regardless of channel size, then having the design collapse under an interviewer's 'what about the company-wide 50,000-person channel' follow-up.

- ⚠️ Ignoring typing indicators and presence as 'just a small feature' when at scale they can generate more raw event volume than actual messages, and need their own lightweight, non-durable delivery path.

> **Model Answer:** The shape of the trade-off is the same, but the fix differs. A feed handles the celebrity case by merging their tweets in at read time. **Q: How would you make search results relevant, not just present, across years of workspace history?**

> **Model Answer:** Beyond basic text matching, a real system ranks by signals like recency, whether the message is in a channel the searching user is active in, and engagement (replies, reactions), and typically restricts results to only channels the user is currently a member of for both relevance and access-control reasons, since showing content from a channel a user isn't in would be a real security bug, not just a UX flaw.

# Design a Video Conferencing System (Zoom)

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Zoom • Google Meet` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The core tension is that every participant's **upload bandwidth** and CPU are fixed and limited, so the real design question isn't 'how do we send video,' it's 'who does the work of combining N video streams into what each participant actually sees,' and the answer changes completely as the participant count grows.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a video conferencing system like Zoom: multiple participants join a
call and can see and hear each other in near real time, with support for
calls ranging from a two-person conversation to a meeting with hundreds of
participants. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the maximum number of participants in a single call we need to support?
*Why it matters:* A handful of participants can be handled by a fundamentally different, much simpler architecture (direct peer-to-peer) than hundreds of participants can, similar to how follower count decides feed architecture. This single number decides the whole media-routing strategy.

#### Q: Do participants need to see everyone at once, or typically just the active speaker plus a few others?

- ⚠️ Forgetting that bandwidth adaptation needs to be per-recipient, not per-call, since different participants have different network conditions simultaneously on the very same call.
- ⚠️ Treating signaling and media as one combined path, when keeping them separate is exactly what lets the system recover from a brief signaling hiccup without dropping the actual audio/video.

> **Model Answer:** In mesh, each participant uploads a separate stream directly to every other participant, so required upload bandwidth and CPU scale linearly with the number of other participants. # Design a Presence System (Online/Offline Status)

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `WhatsApp • Slack • Facebook Messenger` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Presence looks like a tiny piece of state (online or not) but the actual engineering problem is **fan-out**: naively broadcasting every status flip to everyone who might care would generate more traffic than the messages themselves, so the whole design is about ==narrowing who gets told and how often==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design the presence system behind a messaging app: every user's client
shows a green dot next to their contacts who are currently online, and a
"last seen" timestamp for those who aren't. Hundreds of millions of users
may be connected at once, and their status changes constantly. Design the
system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Who actually needs to be notified when a user's status changes: everyone on the platform, or only that user's contacts/open chats?

#### Q: How is 'online' actually detected: a persistent connection, periodic heartbeats, or both?

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**

- Adaptive debounce based on recent flap frequency for that user (longer delay for a user who's flapped repeatedly in the last minute): more resilient to genuinely bad connections, but adds per-user state and tuning complexity that a fixed window avoids

### How do you scope fan-out so a status change doesn't get pushed to a user's entire contact list?

- Polling instead of push (client periodically re-fetches status for visible contacts): removes the need for a subscription registry entirely, but trades push's low latency for polling interval lag, and still costs server load proportional to polling frequency times visible contacts

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The in-memory presence store is read and written on nearly every heartbeat across hundreds of millions of connections; it must be sharded by user_id across a cluster, since a single instance cannot hold that write rate.
- The subscription registry needs fast expiry and cleanup, or stale subscriptions (from crashed clients that never unsubscribed) accumulate and quietly inflate fan-out volume back toward the broadcast case this design is trying to avoid.
- A large group of mutual contacts all opening the same popular user's profile at once (a mini celebrity effect) can spike that one user's fan-out fan-in disproportionately; the pub/sub layer needs to handle a skewed subscriber count per target user gracefully.
- Presence gateways dying takes down their held connections at once, similar to a chat gateway; heartbeat TTL expiry naturally self-heals affected users to offline rather than requiring an explicit failure-detection pass.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Broadcasting every status change to a user's entire contact list==, ignoring that most contacts aren't currently looking, which multiplies fan-out volume for no user-facing benefit.
- ⚠️ ==Treating connection drop as an instant, un-debounced offline signal==, causing visible status to flicker on any user with a shaky connection.
- ⚠️ Storing full presence history durably on every heartbeat, when only the current state and last-seen timestamp actually need to persist beyond an in-memory TTL.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that subscriptions need their own expiry; stale subscriptions from clients that closed without unsubscribing quietly grow fan-out back toward broadcast levels over time.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is TTL-based expiry preferred over explicit disconnect events for detecting offline status?**

> **Model Answer:** A clean disconnect message assumes the client gets a chance to send one, which isn't true for a crashed app, a killed process, or a gateway server that dies mid-connection. **TTL expiry** treats 'absence of a recent heartbeat' as the ground truth instead, so a user is correctly marked offline within one TTL window regardless of how the connection actually ended, with no separate failure-detection system required.

**Q: How would you handle a user with an unusually large number of active subscribers, like a public figure whose status page many people have open at once?**

> **Model Answer:** This is a smaller-scale version of the celebrity fan-out problem: cap or batch fan-out delivery for high-subscriber targets, and consider serving their status via a short-lived cached snapshot refreshed on an interval instead of pushing to every subscriber individually on every flip, trading a little staleness for bounded fan-out cost.

# Design a Group Chat System

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `WhatsApp Groups • Telegram • Discord` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A group chat is Twitter's fan-out problem shrunk down to a **bounded, known-in-advance audience**, and that boundedness is exactly what makes **fan-out-on-write** the right default here, unlike the timeline case where an unbounded, skewed audience forced a hybrid.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Extend a one-on-one messaging system to support group chats: a message
sent to a group must be delivered to every member, each member sees who
has read the message, and groups can range from a handful of friends to
thousands of members. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the group size distribution: mostly small friend groups, or do we need to support large communities of thousands of members?
*Why it matters:* A handful of members and a few thousand members are different engineering problems. Small groups can fan out synchronously and cheaply; large groups start to resemble the celebrity fan-out case and may need the read path involved.

#### Q: Do we need per-member read receipts (who specifically has read the message), or just an aggregate read count?
*Why it matters:* **Per-member receipts** mean tracking one row per (message, member) pair, which for a 500-person group is 500x the bookkeeping of a one-on-one chat. An aggregate count is far cheaper and is what most large-group products actually ship.

#### Q: Can group membership change (people added or removed) while old messages still exist?
*Why it matters:* If a new member should not see history predating their join, delivery and history queries both need to be scoped by 'messages sent after this member joined,' not just 'all messages in this group,' which changes both the write path and the read query.

#### Q: Is delivery ordering required to be identical for every member, or is per-member eventual consistency acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Guaranteeing every member sees messages in the exact same order requires a single ordering authority per group. Accepting minor per-member ordering differences allows a simpler, more parallel fan-out with no shared bottleneck.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can create a group and add or remove members (up to some maximum group size).
- A message sent to a group is delivered to every current member, whether they're online now or offline.
- A sender can see delivery and read status for a group message (either per-member or as an aggregate count, depending on group size).
- A member can view the group's message history from whenever they joined onward.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Message delivery to a small group must feel just as instant as one-on-one messaging.**
- **The system must not let a single very large group's fan-out volume degrade delivery latency for every other, smaller group sharing the same infrastructure.**
- **Read receipt bookkeeping must stay bounded even for groups with thousands of members, rather than growing without limit per message.**
- **A member added to a group must never receive messages sent before they joined.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 500 million total users; 100 million active groups; average group size 8 members, with a long tail up to 10,000 members for large community groups
- An average group sends 30 messages/day; a large (max-size) group sends 500 messages/day

- ⚠️ Treating all groups as the same size for fan-out purposes, letting one very large group's delivery burst add latency to the far more common, much smaller groups sharing the same gateway fleet.

# Design an Email System (Gmail)

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Gmail • Outlook` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Email is really two different systems duct-taped together: a federated, decades-old delivery protocol you don't control (**SMTP**, talking to every other mail server on earth) and a storage-and-search problem you fully control (one mailbox per user, at a scale where a single power user's history can hit millions of messages), and almost every hard decision here is about ==not letting the first system's unreliability leak into the second system's guarantees==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design an email system like Gmail: a user can compose and send an email to
any address on the internet (not just other users of your system), receive
email from any address on the internet, organize a mailbox of potentially
hundreds of thousands of messages, and search across their entire mail
history instantly. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Do we need to interoperate with the broader internet's email system (send to and receive from any external address), or is this a closed system where all users are on our own domain?
*Why it matters:* Interoperating with the real internet means implementing **SMTP** as both a sending and receiving party, dealing with other servers' queuing, retries, and rejections, an entirely different and much harder problem than a closed messaging app that owns both ends of every conversation.

#### Q: What's the expected mailbox size and retention? Are we designing for a mailbox that keeps everything forever, like Gmail's 'never delete' philosophy?
*Why it matters:* **Unlimited retention** turns storage from 'recent hot data' into a problem with a long tail of cold, rarely-accessed data spanning years, which changes the storage tier strategy and the cost model entirely.

#### Q: Does full-text search need to cover the entire mailbox instantly, including attachments, or just recent mail and subject lines?
*Why it matters:* Instant full-text search across a user's entire multi-year history requires a dedicated search index kept in sync with every mailbox mutation, which is a substantial subsystem on its own, not a side feature.

#### Q: How aggressive does spam and phishing filtering need to be, and can it introduce a small amount of delivery latency?
*Why it matters:* A spam pipeline that must complete before a message reaches the inbox adds a processing stage to the critical delivery path, and the accuracy-versus-latency trade-off there shapes whether filtering happens inline or asynchronously after initial delivery.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can compose and send an email to one or more recipients, on this system or any external domain.
- A user can receive email sent to their address from any sender, internal or external.
- A user can organize mail into folders/labels (inbox, sent, spam, trash, custom labels) and mark messages read, starred, or archived.
- A user can search their full mail history by sender, subject, body text, and attachment name, and get results in well under a second.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Delivery must be reliable: a message accepted for sending must eventually be delivered or the sender must be reliably notified of failure, never silently dropped.**
- **Mailbox storage must scale per user to hundreds of thousands of messages and tens of gigabytes of attachments without degrading read or search performance.**
- **The system must be highly available for both receiving mail (an external server sending to us should rarely get a hard failure) and reading mail.**
- **Spam and phishing filtering must catch the large majority of abusive mail without materially delaying legitimate delivery.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 1 billion active mailboxes
- Average user sends 5 emails/day and receives 25 emails/day
- Average email (with metadata, no large attachments) is about 50 KB; roughly 20% of emails carry attachments averaging 2 MB
- Average mailbox retains 5 years of mail before most users stop looking at it, though storage never actually deletes it

# Design a Push Notification Service

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Apple Push Notification service • Firebase Cloud Messaging` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> You never actually deliver a notification to a device, you hand it to whichever **platform-owned gateway** (Apple's, Google's, or a browser vendor's) owns the persistent connection to that device, so the whole design is really about reliably routing to the right gateway, tracking **device tokens** that constantly go stale, and queuing for devices that are offline, not about a real-time delivery pipe you control end to end.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a push notification service that lets any client application (a
ride-sharing app, a social app, a news app) send a notification to a
specific user's phone or browser, even when that app isn't open. The
service must deliver to iOS, Android, and web clients, handle devices that
are offline, and avoid overwhelming a single user with too many
notifications at once. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs

- Rate limiting only per-user: protects the end-user experience, but a burst across many users can still trip the platform gateway's sender-level limits
- Both layers together: gateway-pool rate limiting protects infrastructure-level standing with each platform, per-user capping protects the individual experience; running only one leaves the other failure mode uncovered

- Each platform gateway enforces its own rate limits per sender identity, so the dispatch worker pools must scale and rate-limit independently per gateway, a burst on iOS traffic should never starve or slow down Android/web dispatch.

- ⚠️ Not rate-limiting per gateway, leading to a sender being throttled or temporarily blocked by Apple or Google during a traffic spike.
- ⚠️ Expanding a large campaign into millions of individual queue items eagerly at request time instead of lazily at dispatch time, causing a massive write burst and stale device lookups for a campaign that takes minutes to fully process.

- The practical answer: strict matching as the default, with a time-boxed escalation (e.g. after 60 seconds unmatched, widen the eligible agent pool), giving most chats a good match while bounding worst-case wait time

- Unified record is the stronger choice specifically because handoff fidelity is a functional requirement here, not just an implementation preference; the coupling cost is worth paying for the guarantee

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing routing as simple round-robin or first-available without considering that under real load, strict skill matching can strand visitors in queue while mismatched agents sit idle.
- ⚠️ ==Building the bot conversation and the human agent conversation as two separate systems== bridged only by a summary at handoff time, losing fidelity exactly when a human needs full context.
- ⚠️ ==Treating agent availability as a boolean flag== instead of a load threshold, causing over-assignment once agents are expected to handle multiple concurrent chats.
- ⚠️ Not making the wait queue durable, so a routing service restart during a traffic spike silently drops visitors who were waiting.

**Q: Why is it important that agent availability be read from a fast, low-latency store with atomic claim semantics rather than a general relational table?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the routing decision happens on every new chat and handoff, and a slow or non-atomic read-then-write on agent status creates a **race window** where two chats can both be assigned to the same agent right as they go from available to busy; an atomic claim (e.g. compare-and-swap on current_chat_count against max_concurrent_chats) in a fast in-memory store closes that race, which a slower or non-atomic relational update would not reliably do under concurrent routing requests.

**Q: What's the trade-off in relaxing skill-matching requirements after a wait threshold instead of always requiring a perfect match?**

> **Model Answer:** Always requiring a perfect match guarantees every agent assignment is fully qualified but can leave a visitor waiting a long time if the only matching agents are busy while other, less-matched agents are idle, hurting wait-time SLAs and visitor experience. Relaxing the requirement after a bounded wait trades a small amount of match quality for a bounded worst-case wait time, which is usually the better trade-off since an imperfectly matched but fast human response beats a perfectly matched but very slow one for most support scenarios.

# Design Discord

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Discord` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Discord is really two different real-time systems wearing one UI: **durable, ordered text messaging** per channel, and ==lossy, latency-obsessed voice transport== per channel, and the entire architecture is about keeping those two very different delivery models from being forced through the same pipe.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a system like Discord: users organize into servers (communities),
each server contains multiple text and voice channels, members can send
persistent text messages per channel and join low-latency live voice
calls per channel, and servers have a role-based permission system
controlling who can do what. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Are text and voice genuinely separate subsystems, or does the design need to unify them into a single message/event pipeline?
*Why it matters:* Text needs **durability, ordering, and history**; voice needs ==sub-100ms latency== and can drop packets without anyone caring. Forcing both through one delivery mechanism optimizes for neither, so this decision shapes the entire system split.

#### Q: How large do servers and channels get: is this closer to a few hundred members, or communities with hundreds of thousands?
*Why it matters:* A 200-person server and a 500,000-member server need very different text fan-out and voice-routing strategies. This decides whether we can treat 'channel' as a small bounded audience or need the same large-group handling as a group chat system.

#### Q: For voice, are we relaying audio through our own servers, or can clients connect peer-to-peer for small calls?
*Why it matters:* Peer-to-peer works for a handful of participants but doesn't scale past a small group and has no server-side moderation hook. A server-relayed model (SFU) is what makes large voice channels, recording, and moderation possible at all, at the cost of running real-time media infrastructure.

#### Q: How granular does the permission system need to be: per-server roles only, or per-channel overrides on top of roles?
*Why it matters:* Per-channel overrides on top of server-wide roles is a materially more complex authorization model (effective permission = role permissions merged with channel-specific overrides) than a flat per-server role, and it needs to be checked on every single message send and channel join.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can create a server, and the server can contain multiple text channels and voice channels.
- A member can send a text message in a channel, visible to all members with access to that channel, with persistent history.
- A member can join a voice channel and talk with other members in that same channel in near real time.
- Server owners can define roles with specific permissions (send messages, join voice, manage channels) and assign them to members, with optional per-channel overrides.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Voice audio must have very low, consistent latency (well under 150ms end to end) since gaming and live conversation are unusable otherwise.**
- **Text messages must never be lost or silently reordered within a channel, even if delivered a moment late.**
- **Permission checks must be fast enough to run on every message send and channel action without adding noticeable latency.**
- **The system must isolate a large, extremely active server (a viral community) from degrading performance for every other server sharing the same infrastructure.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 150 million monthly active users; 5 million concurrent voice participants at peak across all servers
- Average server has 50 members and 8 text channels; average text channel gets 500 messages/day
- Voice audio is Opus-encoded at roughly 32 kbps per participant stream
- Average voice call has 4 concurrent speakers per channel at any instant

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Text messages per day and per second:** Assume 10 million active servers * 8 channels * 500 messages/day = 40 billion messages/day ≈ 463,000 messages/sec average, several times that at peak, in the same ballpark as a large-scale group chat system
- **Voice bandwidth per participant (SFU model, receiving N-1 streams):** In a 4-person active voice channel, each client downloads 3 other streams * 32 kbps = 96 kbps down, while uploading 1 stream at 32 kbps, i.e. the server (not the client) bears the N-way fan-out cost
- **Total SFU relay bandwidth at peak concurrency:** 5,000,000 concurrent voice participants * roughly 32 kbps upload received by the SFU = 160 Gbps of inbound audio alone, before the SFU re-distributes it back out to listeners, which roughly doubles again in aggregate egress
- **Voice server (SFU instance) capacity:** A single SFU box handles roughly a few thousand concurrent streams before CPU/bandwidth limits; 5,000,000 / 3,000 ≈ 1,700 SFU instances needed at peak, geographically distributed to keep round-trip latency low

*Capacity Takeaway:* The driving fact is that voice bandwidth and text message volume are two independent scaling problems with different bottlenecks (voice is bounded by **real-time relay bandwidth** and geographic latency, text is bounded by message throughput and storage), which is exactly why the architecture treats them as two separate backend systems rather than one unified pipeline.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Text and voice run as two independent backend paths that only share the
server/channel/permission data model. Text messages flow through a
gateway that checks the sender's effective permission (role bitfield
merged with channel overrides), writes to a channel-sharded message
store, and pushes to the small set of currently-connected members of that
channel, essentially a bounded group chat fan-out. Voice works
differently: joining a voice channel routes the client to a
geographically nearby **SFU** (selective forwarding unit) instance, which
receives each speaker's audio stream once and forwards it to every other
participant, so N participants cost the SFU roughly N inbound and
N*(N-1) outbound relayed streams rather than requiring every client to
connect to every other client directly. Permission checks and channel
membership are the only things both paths depend on.

    voicereg["Voice Session Registry"]:::cache

#### Text channel delivery vs voice channel delivery

### Entity: `servers`
- `server_id`
- `owner_id`
- `name`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* The top-level community container; roles and channels both belong to a server.

### Entity: `channels`
- `channel_id`
- `server_id`
- `type (text | voice)`
- `name`
- `permission_overrides (per-role overrides scoped to this channel)`
*Notes:* A channel's effective permissions are the server role's base permissions merged with any channel-specific overrides, computed at check time, not pre-materialized.

### Entity: `messages`
- `message_id (time-sortable)`
- `channel_id`
- `author_id`
- `text`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* Sharded by channel_id, same reasoning as group chat: a channel's full history should live together for fast range reads.

### Entity: `roles_and_members`
- `server_id`
- `user_id`
- `role_ids (assigned roles)`
- `role permissions (bitfield of allowed actions per role)`
*Notes:* Permissions are stored as a bitfield per role for a fast bitwise check on every action, rather than a database join on every message send.

### Entity: `voice_sessions`
- `channel_id`
- `user_id`
- `sfu_instance_id`
- `joined_at`
*Notes:* Ephemeral, in-memory routing state, same shape as the connection registry in a messaging system: which SFU instance currently holds this user's live audio stream.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Why relay voice through a server (SFU) instead of connecting participants directly (mesh)?
A full mesh, where every participant sends their audio directly to every other participant, requires each client to upload N-1 separate streams, which falls apart past a handful of people (an 8-person call would need each client uploading 7 simultaneous streams). An SFU (selective forwarding unit) has each client upload just one stream to the server, which then forwards it to everyone else, moving the N-way fan-out cost off constrained client uplinks and onto server infrastructure built for it, and giving the server a place to apply moderation, recording, or bandwidth-adaptive forwarding.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Peer-to-peer mesh: lowest possible latency (no relay hop) and zero server bandwidth cost, but upload bandwidth per client scales with participant count, making it unusable past roughly 4-6 people, and offers no server-side moderation hook
- SFU (selective forwarding, server relays without decoding): each client uploads once regardless of channel size, server bears the relay bandwidth cost, and this is what makes large voice channels and moderation features possible at all
- MCU (server decodes and mixes all streams into one combined stream per listener): minimizes client download bandwidth further since each listener gets one mixed stream instead of N separate ones, but costs significant server-side CPU to decode and re-encode audio for every participant, a cost SFU avoids by only forwarding, not transcoding

### How do per-channel permission overrides interact with server-wide roles without a database join on every message?
A member's effective permission in a specific channel is computed by starting from their role's base permission bitfield (say, 'can send messages' is bit 3) and then applying that channel's specific overrides (which might deny bit 3 for a particular role in a specific announcements channel), producing a final allow/deny per action. Storing permissions as bitfields lets this merge happen as a couple of fast bitwise operations in the gateway process, entirely in memory, rather than a database round trip on every single message send.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Bitfield roles with in-memory channel override merge: extremely fast per-action check (no database hit on the hot path), but requires roles and overrides to be cached and invalidated correctly whenever a permission changes, or a stale cache briefly grants access that was just revoked
- Database join computing effective permission on every action: always reflects the latest permission state with no cache invalidation risk, but adds a database round trip to the highest-frequency operation in the whole system (every message send), which doesn't scale
- Pre-materializing effective permissions per (user, channel) pair on every role/override change: keeps the hot path cache-only like the bitfield approach, but multiplies write amplification on every permission change, since one role edit can touch effective-permission rows for every member and every channel that role applies to

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- SFU instances need geographic distribution, since voice latency is dominated by round-trip network distance; a user routed to a far-away SFU will have noticeably worse call quality regardless of how well the SFU itself scales.
- A viral, extremely active server (tens of thousands of members) puts unusual load on both text fan-out (many concurrently connected members per channel) and permission checks (large role/member tables); this server needs to be isolated or the shared gateway fleet degrades for smaller, unrelated servers.
- Voice channel capacity is bounded per SFU instance by both CPU (packet forwarding) and bandwidth (N*(N-1) relayed streams growing quadratically with participants); very large voice channels need either a participant cap or a cascaded multi-SFU relay topology.
- Permission cache invalidation across a distributed gateway fleet must be fast and reliable, since a stale cached permission can incorrectly grant or deny access after a role change, and role changes happen far less often than message sends but must never be silently ignored.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing one unified message pipeline for both text and voice, when their durability, ordering, and latency requirements are different enough to need separate systems entirely.
- ⚠️ Proposing a peer-to-peer mesh for voice without a participant cap, not realizing per-client upload bandwidth scales with participant count and becomes unusable well before typical voice channel sizes.
- ⚠️ Computing effective permissions with a database join on the message-send hot path, adding a round trip to the single highest-frequency operation in the system.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that a role change needs to invalidate cached permissions across every gateway instance, or a revoked permission stays effectively granted until caches happen to expire.

> **Model Answer:** Text fan-out tolerates a small delay and needs durable, ordered delivery, which fits a queue-and-push model well. Voice needs sub-150ms round-trip latency and has no durability requirement at all, dropped packets are simply lost audio, not a bug. Routing voice through the same durable, queued pipeline as text would add latency voice can't tolerate, so it needs its own real-time media relay (SFU) infrastructure instead.

**Q: How would you scale voice channels to support significantly larger participant counts, like a 500-person community voice channel?**

> **Model Answer:** A single SFU's relay cost grows roughly with N participants for upload and N*(N-1) for the total forwarded output, so past some size a single instance can't keep up. Options include cascading multiple SFUs (each handling a subset of participants and relaying a summarized stream between SFU instances), or, more commonly for very large voice audiences, switching listen-only participants to a much cheaper one-way broadcast model rather than full bidirectional relay for everyone.

# Design a Real-Time Collaborative Cursor/Presence System

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Figma • Google Docs` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A chat message that arrives late or slightly out of order is a bug; a cursor position that arrives late or gets dropped is invisible a fraction of a second later anyway, and that single difference is what lets this system trade away every ==durability guarantee== a messaging system treats as non-negotiable in exchange for **raw speed**.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design the system behind the colored cursors and name labels you see
moving around live in tools like Figma or Google Docs: every user viewing
the same document sees every other viewer's live cursor position, updated
many times per second, with minimal visible lag. Design the system end
to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Does a dropped or out-of-order cursor update need to be retried or corrected, or can it simply be superseded by the next one?
*Why it matters:* If the answer is 'just superseded,' the system can use **unreliable, unordered, fire-and-forget delivery**, which is dramatically cheaper and lower-latency than anything with retries or ordering guarantees. This single answer determines the entire transport choice.

#### Q: How many simultaneous collaborators does a single document or room need to support?
*Why it matters:* Broadcasting every cursor move to every other viewer is an **N-to-N fan-out** within the room; a 5-person document and a 500-person live workshop board need very different fan-out strategies, the same way group size drove the fan-out design in a group chat system.

#### Q: Do cursor updates need to be persisted anywhere, or do they only matter for the instant they're displayed?
*Why it matters:* If nobody needs cursor history after the fact, the system needs ==zero durable storage== for this data at all, only a live in-memory broadcast path, which is a fundamentally simpler and cheaper design than anything storing state.

#### Q: Is this purely cursor position, or does it also need to broadcast selections, live edits, and other presence signals through the same channel?
*Why it matters:* Live document edits (the actual content changes) typically need a real **conflict-resolution protocol like OT or CRDTs**, a much heavier guarantee than cursor position. Scoping this to cursor and presence broadcast only keeps the interview focused on the fan-out and freshness problem rather than merging into full collaborative editing.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Every user viewing a document sees a live, moving cursor for every other user currently viewing that same document.
- Each cursor is labeled with the viewer's name or a distinguishing color.
- A cursor disappears promptly when that user closes the document or loses connection.
- Cursor updates feel smooth and immediate, not choppy or laggy, even with several concurrent collaborators.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **End-to-end latency for a cursor update should be **well under 100ms** so movement feels live rather than delayed.**
- **The system must tolerate dropped or out-of-order updates gracefully, since a stale cursor position is meaningless the moment a newer one exists.**
- **Bandwidth and server cost must stay low even at high update rates (many updates per second per user), since this data has no long-term value once displayed.**
- **The system must scale **fan-out within a single room** to at least a few hundred concurrent viewers without degrading update latency for everyone in that room.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 10 million documents open concurrently at peak; average of 3 concurrent viewers per open document, with some documents (workshops, large reviews) having up to 200
- An actively-moving client sends a cursor update roughly 20 times per second, but only a fraction of open viewers are moving their mouse at any instant, say 20% at once
- Each cursor update payload is tiny, roughly 40 bytes (x, y, user_id, color reference)
- The server does not persist any cursor data, only relays it live, so there is no storage growth over time

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Concurrent open documents needing an active broadcast room:** 10,000,000 documents, each an independent fan-out scope; a cursor update from one document's room never needs to reach any other room
- **Inbound update rate across all documents:** 10,000,000 documents * 3 viewers avg * 20% actively moving * 20 updates/sec = 12 million inbound updates/sec system-wide
- **Outbound fan-out rate for an average 3-viewer document:** 1 update from 1 mover is relayed to 2 other viewers = 2 outbound sends per inbound update, roughly doubling the average document's traffic, a small, cheap multiplier at this room size
- **Outbound fan-out rate for a 200-viewer workshop document:** 1 update from 1 mover is relayed to 199 other viewers = 199 outbound sends per inbound update, a ~100x larger fan-out multiplier than the average document, purely from room size

*Capacity Takeaway:* The driving fact is that this system is **bandwidth-and-fan-out bound**, not storage bound: 12 million tiny, disposable updates per second with zero persistence needed is only affordable because nothing here is written to disk, and the fan-out multiplier per update scales directly with how many viewers share a room, which is why large rooms (not total document count) are the real scaling risk.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Each open document maps to a lightweight, **ephemeral broadcast room** held
entirely in memory on one gateway instance (or a small shard of
instances for very large rooms). A client sends cursor position updates
over an open WebSocket using fire-and-forget, unordered, unacknowledged
delivery: no retry, no queue, no durable write. The gateway holding that
room simply overwrites the sender's last-known position in an in-memory
map and immediately broadcasts the new position to every other connected
member of the same room. If an update is dropped, nothing recovers it,
the next update a fraction of a second later simply supersedes it. When
a client disconnects, the gateway removes their entry and broadcasts a
"cursor left" event, and the room itself is discarded once its last
member leaves.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Ephemeral room broadcast, no durable writes

```mermaid
flowchart LR

    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    clienta["Client A (moving)"]:::client
    clientb["Client B (viewing)"]:::client
    gw["Room Gateway"]:::server
    roomstate["In-memory Room State"]:::cache
    registry["Room Membership Registry"]:::cache
    clienta -->|"cursor update (fire-and-forget)"| gw
    gw -->|"overwrite last position"| roomstate
    gw -.->|"broadcast (batched tick)"| clientb
    gw -->|"track room membership"| registry
```

#### A cursor update travels from mouse move to another viewer's screen

#### Outbound fan-out grows linearly with room size

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `WS` | `wss://rooms/{documentId}/connect` | Joins the live broadcast room for a document; the server assigns the client a color/identity and immediately sends the current set of active cursors in that room. |
| `WS` | `wss://rooms/{documentId}/cursor` | **Fire-and-forget** message sent over the open socket with the client's latest { x, y } position; no acknowledgment is sent back, and only the most recent position per user matters. |
| `GET` | `/api/rooms/{documentId}/active` | Fallback HTTP snapshot of who's currently active in the room (used for initial paint before the socket finishes connecting, or for clients that don't need live cursors, only a viewer count). |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `active_room_state`
- `document_id (key)`
- `user_id`
- `x, y (last known position)`
- `color`
- `updated_at`
*Notes:* Entirely **in-memory**, held only for the lifetime of the room being active; never written to durable storage, since a cursor position has no value once superseded or once the last viewer leaves.

### Entity: `room_membership`
- `document_id (key)`
- `user_id`
- `gateway_id`
- `connected_at`
*Notes:* Tracks which broadcast gateway instance holds a given room's connections, so the room can be torn down cleanly the moment the last member disconnects.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Why is unreliable, unordered, fire-and-forget delivery the right choice here when it would be unacceptable for chat messages?
A chat message is meaningful forever: losing one is a permanent, visible gap in the conversation, so messaging systems pay for durability, retries, and strict ordering. A cursor position's value ==decays to zero== within a fraction of a second, since a newer position immediately supersedes it. Retrying a dropped cursor update after the fact would deliver a position that's already stale and wrong, actively worse than just letting it be superseded by whatever the next update says. This is the core reason the transport can drop the guarantees a messaging system treats as load-bearing.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Reliable, ordered delivery (like a message queue with acks and retries): guarantees every update arrives, but adds latency and complexity for data that's obsolete within milliseconds of being generated, actively counterproductive here
- Unreliable, unordered, fire-and-forget (e.g. plain WebSocket sends, or UDP-based transport where available): lowest possible latency and server overhead, occasional dropped or reordered updates are invisible since only the latest position ever matters
- Client-side interpolation/extrapolation on top of unreliable delivery: smooths out visible jumps from dropped updates by estimating motion between the last two known points, adding a little client complexity in exchange for the appearance of smoothness even under real-world packet loss

### How do you keep a 200-person room's fan-out from overwhelming the gateway or flooding every client's bandwidth?
Naively broadcasting every single cursor update at full frequency to every other member scales as roughly **(active movers) times (room size)**, which grows fast for large rooms. Two levers bring this down: throttling how often a client sends updates (e.g. capping to 10-20/sec regardless of raw mouse event rate) and batching/coalescing outbound broadcasts per room on a fixed tick (e.g. broadcast the latest known state of all movers every 50ms as one batched message, rather than relaying each individual update immediately as it arrives).

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Broadcast every update immediately, unbatched: lowest possible per-update latency, but fan-out volume scales directly with both room size and per-user update frequency, becoming expensive fast in large rooms
- Client-side send throttling only: reduces the inbound update rate cleanly, but doesn't address outbound fan-out multiplying by room size for large rooms
- Server-side batched broadcast ticks (coalesce all changes in a room into one message every fixed interval): caps outbound message count regardless of how many individual cursors moved, trading a small, usually imperceptible fixed delay (the tick interval) for a large reduction in total messages sent, especially valuable in large rooms

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single very large room (a workshop with hundreds of live viewers) can ==flood== one gateway instance with fan-out traffic; large rooms may need to be sharded across multiple gateway instances with a lightweight relay between them, rather than assuming one room always fits on one machine.
- Because no cursor state is durably persisted, a gateway instance crashing simply drops that room's live state entirely; clients reconnect, rejoin the room, and rebuild presence from scratch, which is acceptable precisely because none of this data had lasting value to begin with.
- Update frequency per client must be **capped server-side** (not just trusted client-side), or a single misbehaving or malicious client can flood a room's fan-out well past its intended rate.
- As concurrent document count grows into the tens of millions, the total number of ephemeral in-memory rooms (even if each is individually cheap) becomes a fleet-wide memory and connection-count planning problem, similar in shape to the persistent-connection scaling challenge in a chat gateway fleet.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Reaching for a reliable, ordered message queue== for cursor updates out of habit, adding latency and complexity for data that's obsolete within milliseconds regardless.
- ⚠️ ==Broadcasting every raw mouse-move event unthrottled==, generating far more update traffic than a smooth-looking cursor actually requires.
- ⚠️ Persisting cursor positions to a database, mistaking 'real-time' data for data that needs to survive past the moment it's displayed.
- ⚠️ Assuming small and large rooms have the same fan-out cost, and not accounting for the fact that fan-out volume grows with room size, not with total number of open documents.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is it acceptable for this system to drop updates that a messaging system would never be allowed to drop?**

> **Model Answer:** A chat message has permanent value: losing it is a visible, permanent gap. A cursor position's value is entirely tied to being **the most recent one**; the instant a newer position exists, the old one is worthless, whether or not it was ever delivered. Retrying a dropped cursor update would just deliver stale, wrong data late, which is worse than doing nothing, so the system is designed to let newer updates simply supersede lost ones rather than guarantee delivery of every single one.

**Q: How would you handle a room with hundreds of concurrent live viewers without overwhelming the gateway?**

> **Model Answer:** Two levers: **throttle** how often each client is allowed to send updates regardless of raw mouse event rate, and switch the server's outbound broadcast from per-update relay to a fixed-interval **batched tick** that coalesces every room member's latest position into one message. Both cap the fan-out multiplier that would otherwise grow linearly with room size, at the cost of a small, generally imperceptible fixed delay from the batching interval.
